Why this exists

Ottawa acknowledges Algonquin territory every day.

Land acknowledgements are spoken in government buildings, universities, conferences and public events across the capital. They matter. But acknowledgement and presence are not the same thing.

Walk through downtown Ottawa and there are remarkably few permanent, highly visible places where Algonquin people are working, selling, creating and participating in the everyday commercial life of our own traditional territory.

I want people to see something else too: Algonquin cooks. Algonquin entrepreneurs. Algonquin businesses. Algonquin people building something.

One contribution. Two results.

Do something useful now. Build something bigger next.

This campaign is deliberately simple: every contribution creates an immediate food commitment while also helping move a longer-term economic presence project forward.

Right now

Food distributed downtown.

For every $5 contributed, Chelsea's Kitchen commits to distributing one portion of baked bannock and chili in downtown Ottawa in early October, with a focus on the Rideau Street corridor between Augusta and Cobourg.

The longer-term goal

Visible Algonquin entrepreneurship.

Contributions also support the work of developing mobile commercial carts intended to create accessible, highly visible spaces where Algonquin entrepreneurs can test ideas, sell products and begin building businesses.

The bigger project

The cart is more than a food stand.

A downtown storefront can require enormous upfront cost before a new entrepreneur sells a single product. A professionally built mobile cart creates another route: smaller infrastructure, strategic location and a chance to prove an idea.

1
Lower the barrier.

Create an accessible way to test a business idea without needing a full storefront.

2
Put opportunity where people can see it.

The location matters. Visibility in Ottawa's economic and tourism core is part of the point.

3
Make the platform bigger than Chelsea's Kitchen.

The long-term vision is for carts to create opportunities for other Algonquin entrepreneurs as well.

Read the Full Project Story
Why food distribution?

The project isn't about hiding people who are struggling.

It is about adding another visible story. Chelsea's Kitchen has already used food to connect with people downtown. During TRC Week, this campaign can have an immediate impact while we work toward something longer-term.

Every $5 contribution represents a promise to put one portion of food directly into someone's hands.

Build something for tomorrow. Do something useful today.
Who's behind it

I'm trying to build the first version and prove the idea can work.

I'm Kris Odjick, an Algonquin entrepreneur from Kitigan Zibi and the person behind Chelsea's Kitchen.

Chelsea's Kitchen started with baked bannock, community meals and a belief that food can create connection. It has grown into catering, events and a larger question: can small-scale entrepreneurship become part of restoring visible Algonquin economic presence in Ottawa?

Transparency

Where does the money go?

Contributions are made to Chelsea's Kitchen. They are not charitable donations and do not qualify for charitable tax receipts.

For every $5 contributed through this campaign, Chelsea's Kitchen commits to distributing one portion of baked bannock and chili in downtown Ottawa in early October.

Campaign funds also support the work involved in developing the Restoring Algonquin Presence initiative, including food, supplies, equipment, cart development, outreach and related project costs.

This page describes a small-business contribution campaign and an evolving long-term project. Proposed cart locations and partnerships are goals and may change as agreements, permissions and funding develop.
